newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - UK petrol station decline slowing - Conoco.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - UK petrol station decline slowing - Conoco.

text.p: The number of petrol stations in Britain is set to fall by about a third in the next five years in the face of fierce price competition but the decline will be far slower than previously expected, a senior oil company official said on Friday.

"There were about 15,900 last year...I think we'll come down to about 10,000 in the next four to five years," said Steve Theede, managing director and chief executive officer of Conoco Ltd, a unit of U.S. oil major Conoco Inc.
Conoco is itself a unit of Dupont Co.

"But the rate of these closures will not be nearly as fast as most people had previously forecast... We will have the same number of closures at the end of the day but it's a question of pace," he told Reuters in an interview at the inauguration of a new waste-water treatment plant at Conoco's Humber refinery.

Many petrol retailers and oil companies in Britain have been hit in the pockets since the launch by Esso last year of its PriceWatch campaign, a move many observers said was intended to shake a lot of the smaller operators out of the market.
"The agreements most of these small operators have with their suppliers give some kind of a guideline margin," Theede said.
"The suppliers seem to be taking more of a hit in order to allow these small operators to continue to work...Some suppliers are concerned about losing more volume and more market share.
"I think the question is how long the suppliers are prepared to take this disproportionate hit on margins," he added.

Conoco's 170,000 barrels per day Humber refinery, which Theede said was already ranked by finance house Salomon Bros as the most profitable refinery in Europe recently completed upgrading work to improve its margins further.

An 85 million stg vacuum unit started up a few weeks ago at the refinery which will allow one crude unit, responsible for around one third of the refinery's total feedstock throughput, to process North Sea high acidity crudes.
It is the only unit in Europe which can handle a diet of 100 percent high acidity crude, which trades at a discount of around $1.50 to Brent.
"We enjoy around 65 to 75 percent of that $1.50 in terms of margins," Theede said.

But he declined to be precise as to how much Conoco's margins had improved overall as a result of this year's upgrading work which included changes to the refinery's distillate output to comply with tighter EU requirements on sulphur content.
Theede did not foresee any significant changes in the next few years to the British demand pattern for his refinery's product.

"I don't see any significant changes in the next few years but we might see the recent decline in gasoline demand come to a halt and the astronomical diesel demand growth of the last five years begin to moderate a bit," he said.
"We have seen something of an uptick in terms of demand for gasoline, something like 0.6 percent, compared with the four percent that we've been going down in the last two years.

"This may be the result of conversion to diesel cars slowing down firstly because the UK government equalised duty between diesel and unleaded petrol in the Budget two years ago and secondly because over the last year the whole impression that diesel is more environmentally friendly than petrol has been severely challenged," he told Reuters.
